# The Scale-Span Rule {#sec-scale-span}

Chapter 2 proposed a rule, and this chapter is where it has to defend itself.

The rule is short. **An exponent may be reported only together with the span of scales over which
it was fitted, and a span below two orders of magnitude may not be reported as a property of the
object.** Everything else in this chapter is either the reasoning behind it, an attack on it, or a case where it fires wrongly. All three are needed.

I put the rule in a chapter of its own because it is the first device in this book that constrains
what other people are allowed to say. Rules that constrain speech deserve more scrutiny than
observations that describe the world, and I would rather state the attacks myself than wait for
them.

## What the rule is, and what it is not

Three clarifications, because most objections I have received turn out to be about something else.

**It is a reporting convention, not a statistical test.** The distinction matters. It does not tell you whether an exponent
exists. It tells you what you may call it once you have estimated one.

**It applies to exponents, not to power laws as models.** Models with a power-law component can be
fitted to any series at any span. The rule constrains the interpretation of the fitted exponent,
not the fitting.

**It binds the claim, not the study.** The study survives. The claim changes. A short-span study remains useful: it can report a local
slope, compare two objects whose measurements were made the same way, or serve as a diagnostic of
regime change. What it cannot do is report the exponent as a fact about the object.

That last distinction is the one that matters in practice, and it is the reason the rule is not as
restrictive as it sounds.

## Why a span requirement is necessary

The difficulty is elementary. It is also routinely ignored.

Any smooth function looks like a power law over a sufficiently short interval. Take a parabola:
over a small enough window, on log-log axes, it is straight, and its slope is a number you can
report. That number is not the parabola's exponent, because a parabola does not have one. It is the
parabola's local behaviour in the window.

Now extend the reasoning. If a short window makes a parabola look like a power law, then a short
window makes almost anything look like a power law. The fitted exponent, in that window, is a joint
property of the object and the window, and there is no way to separate them from the data alone.

| Object | Local log-log slope over one decade | True power-law exponent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parabola | Approximately 2 (in the domain where it dominates) | Does not exist |
| Exponential decay | Varies continuously with the window | Does not exist |
| Logistic curve | Changes sign across the window | Does not exist |
| True power law | Constant across all windows | The fitted value |

The table's fourth row is the point: the power law is the only member of the family whose local
slope is window-invariant. **That invariance is the property you are trying to detect, and you
cannot detect it inside a window.**

## Three attacks on the rule

**Attack one: precision substitutes for span.** If the data are measured with negligible error and
the window is short, surely a clean fit identifies the exponent?

Response: precision reduces one of the three error sources from the previous chapter, and it is the
source the rule is not about. The problem with a short span is not that the points are noisy. It is
that the alternative models predict the same thing over that span. A perfect measurement of a
logistic curve over one decade is a perfect measurement that cannot distinguish the logistic curve
from a power law.

**Attack two: the rule disqualifies legitimate research.** A great deal of published work in
materials science, physiology, and finance rests on exponents fitted over one to two decades.

Response: partly true, and the rule's effect is narrower than the objection assumes. Most of that
work uses exponents comparatively, in the descriptive sense described in Chapter 2. Those
conclusions survive; what changes is the wording. A smaller subset treats the exponent as a model
input, and for those the objection is valid, and the work is affected. **I accept the implication
rather than soften the rule.**

**Attack three: any threshold is arbitrary.** Why two decades rather than three, or one and a half?

Response: correct, and conceded in advance. It always is. The threshold is a convention, chosen because a decade
is roughly the span over which the curvature of a plausible alternative becomes visible in a
log-log plot. The rule's content is the reporting requirement. A reader who prefers a different
threshold has kept the substance and changed the number, which is the intended outcome.

## Two cases where the rule fires wrongly

A rule that never misfires is not a rule. It is a slogan. Here are two false positives.

**Case one: an object with a genuine characteristic scale.** Some systems have a dominant length
scale and no scaling regime at all. The rule would classify their fitted exponents as window
descriptions, which is technically right and substantively unhelpful, because the correct statement
is not "the exponent is a description of the window" but "this object has no exponent."

The rule needs a companion: if the object has a characteristic scale, do not fit a power law. The
checklist in Chapter 2 covers this at step four, which is why step four exists.

**Case two: the decisions do not depend on the exponent.** A process engineer may need to know only
that roughness is high rather than low, and may not care whether the exponent is 1.6 or 1.9. Under
those conditions the rule's insistence on the span is pedantic: the uncertainty is irrelevant to
the decision.

I accept the case and draw a different conclusion from it than the objector would. When the
decision is robust to the exponent's uncertainty, the finding should be reported as a **bound** —
"the exponent is above 1.5" — which the rule permits and which is more useful than a point estimate
anyway.

## Is the rule itself a constant?

The book's own device should be applied to the book's own rule, or the device is a decoration.

**What transformation should the rule survive?** If it is a genuine constant, it should hold across
domains: the same reporting standard for exponents in finance, in materials, in traffic data, in
biology.

**Does it?** Partly. The reporting requirement holds everywhere. The threshold's calibration does not: what
counts as an adequate span differs between a system with physical limits at both ends and one
measured by an instrument with a known resolution.

So the rule is a **Grade II constant**: the requirement survives the change of domain, and the
number attached to it does not. That is the same grade as the claim "tails are thick," and it is
the grade at which I would advise readers to hold it.

## Claim and tool

The claim embedded in the rule is that for scale-dependent quantities, the span is part of the
measurement. I regard this as established by the elementary argument above rather than as a
proposal.

The tool is the reporting convention, and it is a proposal. It is registered as entry B-008 with
its preconditions, and it has been applied to every exponent quoted in this book.

I should note what the rule does for the book's own credibility. It removes from my vocabulary a
class of sentence that is otherwise very tempting: "the exponent is X," with no window. Having
given up those sentences, I have also given up the ability to look more precise than the evidence
allows, which is a useful constraint to accept in public.

## Boundary conditions

The rule presumes that a scale span can be measured and stated, which excludes series with unknown
or changing sampling resolution.

It presumes that a single exponent is the object of interest. Where the relationship is piecewise —
different exponents in different regimes — the span must be reported per regime, and the rule's
threshold applies to each piece.

And it presumes that the reader will use the span. A convention that is not enforced by readers
does nothing, which is why the last section of this chapter is the one that matters most.

## What a reader can do

Three actions, in increasing order of effort.

**Ask for the span.** When someone reports an exponent, ask over what range. The question takes a
sentence and it is usually unanswerable from the published text, which is itself informative.

**Ask what else fits.** A stretched exponential, a lognormal, or a mixture will often fit as well
over the reported span. If the conclusion depends on the choice, the span is carrying more weight
than the data.

**Ask what changes if the exponent is wrong by 30 percent.** If nothing changes, report a bound and
move on. If something changes, the estimation problem is the finding, and the chapter's job is to
say so.

## Calibrating a span

The scale-span rule says that a scale-invariant claim must state the range over which it holds. This
section is about how to choose the range and what to do when the data do not offer a good one.

**The trade-off is unavoidable.** Both ways cost something. A short span gives an estimate computed from data that are
relatively homogeneous, at the cost of few points on the log-log line and an estimate dominated by
noise. A long span gives more leverage on the slope, at the cost of mixing regimes that may not share
a single exponent.

**Three orders of magnitude is a working minimum** for the applications in this book, and it is a
convention rather than a result. The Nile records span more than that; high-frequency financial data
over a decade span about eight orders of magnitude in time, though not all of it is usable; a
three-year sample of daily data spans roughly a single order, which is why claims of long memory from
such samples should be treated as hypotheses rather than estimates.

**Four checks before accepting a span.**

**Do the points lie on a line?** Look at the residuals. Fit, then look at the residuals. Curvature within the span means the
span contains a boundary, and the boundary is the finding.

**Does the slope survive shortening?** Recompute and compare. Recompute with the upper and lower thirds removed. An estimate
that moves by more than the decision's tolerance is not a stable description of the span.

**Are the points independent?** Usually they are not. If the series has long memory, successive observations carry
overlapping information and the effective number of independent points is far smaller than the count
suggests. The uncertainty on the slope is correspondingly larger, and this is the most commonly
omitted correction in applied work.

**Does the span contain the range the decision cares about?** Often it does not. A well-measured exponent over three
orders of magnitude that does not include the horizon of the decision is a description of the wrong
interval. This is the point of stating the range at all.

**What to do when the span is short.** Report the estimate with the range, mark it as provisional, and
treat it as one input among the structural considerations rather than as a parameter. Where a decision
depends on behaviour outside the measured range, the honest output is a bound derived from
considerations that do not require extrapolation — which is what the fourth quadrant's rules are for.
**A short span is not a failure of method. Treating a short span as though it were a long one is.**

## The rule in one page

The scale-span rule has been stated in this chapter and used throughout the book. For reference, the
whole rule in a page.

**State the range. Always.** A scale-invariant description is meaningful over an interval, and the
interval is part of the claim rather than a detail of the method.

**State the procedure.** Stepping, covering and spectral estimates measure different properties. The
procedure belongs next to the number.

**Check stability within the range.** Recompute with the extremes discarded. A slope that moves by more
than the decision's tolerance is not a description of the interval.

**Correct for dependence.** Where the series has long memory, successive observations overlap and the
effective sample is smaller than the count. **The uncertainty is larger than the naive calculation
reports, and this correction is the one most often omitted.**

**Report the sensitivity.** What changes in the decision if the exponent is at the low end of its
range rather than the point estimate. Where nothing changes, the estimation problem does not matter.

**Say when the range is short. Explicitly.** A span of one order of magnitude supports a provisional
statement, not a conclusion. **The failure mode is not a short span; it is treating a short span as a
long one.**

**Why one page.** Because the rule is applied by people who will not read a chapter before using it,
and a rule that requires a chapter to state is a rule that will be applied from memory and get the
range wrong. **One page is the length at which a practitioner can actually check what they did.**

## Two spans in one series

The rule's most useful application is not to a single measured range but to a series that contains two.

**The pattern.** A financial series measured over decades and over minutes often displays different
scaling in the two regimes, with a boundary somewhere between. The boundary is not an artefact; it is
usually the scale at which a different mechanism takes over.

**Three examples of the mechanism change.**

**Microstructure.** At very short horizons, the discreteness of prices and the mechanics of order
matching dominate, producing a scaling that has nothing to do with the process the analyst is studying.

**Institutional rhythm.** Daily and weekly horizons contain reporting cycles, settlement conventions and
scheduled announcements, which introduce periodicities absent at other scales.

**Aggregation.** At long horizons, the series is an average over regimes, and the scaling reflects the
regime distribution rather than the dynamics within any regime.

**What the analyst should do.** Fit each regime separately, and report the boundary with its uncertainty.
**A single exponent fitted across a boundary is a number that describes neither regime, which is why
looking at the residual plot is not optional.**

**Why the boundary is the interesting object.** Because it locates the scale at which one mechanism gives
way to another, and that location is a substantive finding about the market or system. **The exponent
describes the regimes; the boundary describes the machinery.**

**The practical consequence for decisions.** A decision whose horizon sits near a boundary is a decision
whose inputs are least reliable, because small errors in the boundary location change which regime's
estimate applies. **Where that is the case, the honest output is a bound that holds under either regime
rather than an estimate from one.**

## Reporting a scaling result

The rule prescribes what to report. A template, because the format is what gets adopted.

**One sentence of result.** Slope, uncertainty, range. The slope, its uncertainty, and the range over which it was measured.

**One sentence of method.** Procedure and parameters. The procedure and its parameters, including the cut-off and the fitting weight.

**One sentence of stability.** Extremes discarded. The slope recomputed with the extremes discarded, and the difference.

**One sentence of dependence.** Effective count. The effective sample size, where the series is dependent.

**One sentence of sensitivity.** What changes. What changes in the decision if the slope sits at the low end of its range
rather than the point estimate.

**One sentence of duration.** And its monitor. What has to stay the same for the scaling to persist, and how that would be
monitored.

**Six sentences, and the result is usable.** A reader can check the method, audit the stability, apply the
sensitivity and set a review condition. **None of the six requires a new analysis; all of them require the
analysis to have been done with the six questions in mind.**

**What the template replaces.** The paragraph that reports a slope significant at some level, names the
estimator, and stops. **That paragraph is compatible with every one of the six sentences being false, which
is the problem with the convention rather than with any particular paper.**

**Why templates work.** Because a reporting format is a checklist that survives contact with a deadline. **A
rule stated in prose is honoured by the careful and forgotten by everyone under time pressure; a format is
honoured by the fact that the field is empty.**

## The rule and the sample size

The span rule is about the range of measurement and the statistical power question is about the number of
observations. The two interact, and the interaction explains why some scaling results are unstable.

**The interaction. Two senses of more data.**

**More observations within a fixed range.** This improves the estimate's precision. **It does not extend the
range, and the range is what licenses a claim.**

**A wider range with the same number of observations.** This extends the claim's scope and coarsens the estimate.
**The two kinds of improvement trade off, and a study cannot have both without more total data.**

**Three consequences.**

**A long sample at one frequency does not extend the span.** High-frequency data over a year and daily data
over a decade have different ranges and different precisions, and neither substitutes for the other.

**Pooling across instruments is not the same as a wider window.** Cross-sectional pooling increases the number
of observations at each scale; it does not extend the scales covered.

**A claim about behaviour outside the measured span requires an assumption, not more data.** Extrapolation is a
statement about a mechanism, and no additional observation inside the span supports it.

**What to record.** The range, the number of observations, and whether the claim extends beyond the range. **The
third item is the one that is usually left to the reader, and it is the one that decides whether the result is a
measurement or an extrapolation.**

**Why this matters for the book's material.** Because tail and memory claims are frequently made across ranges
where the evidence is thin, and the sample-size question is often invoked as though it addressed the range.
**Two different shortages, and only one of them is fixed by collecting more of the same thing.**

## The span rule and three kinds of exponent

The rule applies to any scale-dependent quantity. Three kinds appear in the book's material, and each has a
characteristic failure.

**A dimension. Geometric.** Estimated by stepping, covering, or spectral methods, with the span measured in the
units of the object. **The characteristic failure is measuring below the resolution of the source data, which
measures the map rather than the object.**

**A tail index. Distributional.** Estimated from the largest observations, with the span measured in ranks or in
the size of the deviations. **The characteristic failure is a cut-off chosen to make the log-log plot look
straight.**

**A memory parameter. Temporal.** Estimated from the autocorrelation structure, with the span measured in lags.
**The characteristic failure is a bandwidth chosen without regard to the dependence being measured, and the
competing explanations of non-stationarity.**

**What the three have in common. Two things.**

**The span is a choice and it belongs in the report.** For the dimension, the range of rulers; for the index, the
cut-off; for memory, the bandwidth. **Three different names for the same requirement.**

**The competing explanations are structural.** A boundary in a scaling relation, a non-stationarity, an
aggregation effect. **Each is a mechanism claim and none is ruled out by more data within the same span.**

**What differs across the three. The remedy for a short span.** A dimension can be measured with a finer ruler
if the source data allow. A tail index cannot manufacture observations. A memory parameter can sometimes use a
longer series at a lower frequency. **Which makes the three failures differently repairable, and the differences
are worth a reader's attention because they determine what a study can fix.**

**Why the three kinds are worth naming together.** Because the rule is stated once in the book and applied three
times, and the applications differ in what can be repaired. **Three names, one requirement, three remedies.**

## The span rule and three ways to report a window

The rule requires the window. Three ways of reporting it appear in practice, and they are not equally useful.

**The range of measurement. Necessary.** "Between scales A and B." **Which is the minimum and is often the only
thing reported.**

**The range of validity. Stronger.** "The relationship holds between A and B and fails outside them." **Which
requires testing past the boundary and is the version a decision needs.**

**The range of applicability. The most useful.** "The decision's horizon lies inside the range." **Which connects
the window to the purpose and is the sentence that determines whether the measurement is relevant.**

**What the three report. Increasingly more work.** The first is a by-product of the fitting; the second requires
an additional test; the third requires knowing what the decision depends on. **Which is why the third is rare and
why it is the one that changes a decision.**

**How to use the three in a document. One sentence each.** Which is three sentences and reads as a complete
scaling result. **"Measured between A and B. The relationship appears to fail below A. The decision's horizon sits
inside the range, so the measurement applies."**

**What the third sentence adds. One thing.** It states that the measurement is relevant, rather than leaving a
reader to compare the ranges. **Which is the step that most often goes unperformed, because the analyst knows the
horizon and the reader does not.**

**What to do when the horizon falls outside.** Report the bound rather than the estimate. **Which is the same
substitution the book makes for non-estimable quantities, and it is what the third sentence makes visible.**

**Why the three ways are worth separating.** Because the rule requires the window and the requirement is satisfied
by any of the three, while only the third makes the result usable. **Three sentences, increasing work, and the
third is the one a decision needs.**

## The span rule and three ways a span is chosen

The rule requires a range and does not say how to choose it. Three selection procedures appear in the material,
and each has a bias.

**By the data's resolution. Mechanical.** The span runs from the finest measurable scale to the coarsest. **Which
is defensible and produces a span determined by instrumentation rather than by the question.**

**By the straight part of the plot. Circular.** The span is chosen where the log-log relation looks linear. **Which
produces a good fit and no information, because the search for linearity has consumed the evidence for it.**

**By the decision's horizon. Purposeful.** The span is chosen to contain the range the decision depends on. **Which
is the only one of the three that connects the measurement to its use, and it can produce a span too short to
estimate the slope.**

**What the three imply. One requirement.** Report which procedure was used. **"Data-determined" and
"purpose-determined" are different claims about the same number.**

**How to combine them. One sequence.** Choose by the horizon, then check whether the resulting span supports an
estimate. **Where it does not, report the horizon requirement and the shortfall rather than extending the
span.**

**Why the circular procedure is the most common.** Because it produces the most convincing plot. **Which is the
reason it is dangerous: a span selected for linearity cannot be used to test linearity.**

**What to record. Two items per span.** The selection procedure and the shortfall if any. **Which is a clause and
which makes the number's provenance available to a reader who will otherwise assume the span was chosen for
statistical reasons.**

## The span rule and three questions from a reviewer

A reviewer receiving a scaling result asks three questions, and each is answerable from the report.

**What range, and how was it chosen.** Not only the numbers: the procedure that produced them. **A span chosen for
the straightness of the plot cannot be used to test straightness, and the procedure is the only way to tell.**

**What happens at the edges.** Whether the relationship was tested beyond the span, and what the residual plot
showed. **Curvature within the span means a boundary, and a boundary is a finding rather than a defect.**

**Does the span contain the decision's horizon.** Which is the applicability question and the one that determines
whether the measurement is relevant. **A well-measured exponent outside the horizon is a description of the wrong
interval.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is answerable from what a competent report contains: the
range, the method, the residual behaviour, and the decision. **Which is why the four-sentence form of the earlier
section is what a reviewer needs rather than a table.**

**Which question is most often unanswerable. The third.** Because it requires the analyst to know what the decision
depends on. **And it is the question that decides whether the work is relevant, which is why the chapter's
practical advice is to write the horizon into the report.**

**What a reviewer should do when the third cannot be answered.** Ask for the horizon rather than for more
analysis. **The information is in the decision, not in the data, and the request costs nothing.**

**Why the three questions are worth stating.** Because the rule requires a window and the requirement is satisfied
by a range alone. **Three questions, and the third is the one that turns a measurement into a usable
result.**
## A note on what this chapter could not check

This chapter is a construction, and the honest statement is that its central argument is elementary
rather than empirical: smooth functions have local log-log slopes. The table is illustrative, and
the fitted-slope values in the middle column are described qualitatively rather than computed here,
because the exact slope depends on the window chosen, which is the point.

The two false positives are cases I have encountered in reading, not a systematic survey. A proper
test of the rule would take a corpus of published exponents, extract the reported spans, and
measure how often the conclusion depends on the fit window. I have not run that study, and the rule
would be better if someone did.
